questions.stem: In Carl Rogers' humanistic theory, the self-concept is best described as:
options: a person's organised set of beliefs and perceptions about who they are
the unconscious part of the mind that holds repressed wishes and fears
a fixed set of inherited traits that is measured by a personality test
the stage of development reached by resolving a psychosocial crisis
questions.explanation: Rogers saw the self-concept as the organised, consistent set of perceptions a person holds about themselves. Unconscious repressed wishes belong to Freud's psychodynamic theory, and resolving psychosocial crises belongs to Erikson.

questions.stem: Leila sees herself as a lazy student, but believes she ought to be a hardworking high achiever. Rogers would describe the gap between these two views as:
options: an identity crisis between industry and inferiority
a conflict between her id and her superego
a deficiency need that is blocking her self-actualisation
incongruence between her self-image and her ideal self
questions.explanation: For Rogers, incongruence is a mismatch between how a person sees themselves (self-image) and who they think they should be (ideal self), and a large gap is linked to anxiety. Id and superego conflict is Freud's language, not Rogers'.

questions.stem: A parent tells a child, 'I love you no matter what, even when I'm unhappy with what you did.' In Rogers' terms the parent is showing:
options: unconditional positive regard
a condition of worth
vicarious reinforcement
reaction formation
questions.explanation: Unconditional positive regard is acceptance of the person regardless of their behaviour, which Rogers believed helps a child develop a congruent self-concept. A condition of worth is the opposite: love that depends on meeting others' standards.

questions.stem: Tom's parents praise him only when he wins at sport, so he comes to believe he is worthless unless he wins. According to Rogers, what is the likely effect?
options: His superego becomes too weak, so he acts on impulses without feeling any guilt at all
He will be fixated at the oral stage, which shows up later as competitive behaviour
Conditions of worth lead him to deny experiences that do not fit, producing incongruence
Conditional praise builds a strong ideal self, which guarantees later self-actualisation
questions.explanation: Rogers argued that conditions of worth teach a person to value themselves only when meeting others' standards, so experiences that do not fit are distorted or denied, widening the gap between self and experience. Fixation and the superego are Freudian ideas.

questions.stem: Which list gives Maslow's hierarchy of needs from the base to the top?
options: Esteem, safety, physiological, love and belonging, self-actualisation
Physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualisation
Safety, physiological, esteem, love and belonging, self-actualisation
Physiological, love and belonging, safety, self-actualisation, esteem
questions.explanation: Maslow placed physiological needs at the base, then safety, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualisation at the top. He proposed that lower (deficiency) needs generally have to be largely met before growth towards self-actualisation becomes a priority.

questions.stem: A common criticism of Maslow's hierarchy as an account of identity is that:
options: it claims identity is fixed by the end of early childhood
people sometimes pursue creativity or meaning while basic needs are unmet
it explains behaviour entirely in terms of rewards and punishments
it was based on large random samples drawn from many cultures
questions.explanation: People such as artists living in poverty pursue higher needs before lower ones are met, which challenges a strict ordering. Maslow built the idea of self-actualisation from a small, selected group of admired people, not from large random cross-cultural samples.

questions.stem: In Freud's structural model of personality, the ego operates on:
options: the morality principle, holding the values learnt from parents and from society
the consistency principle, keeping beliefs in line with each other
the reality principle, balancing the id's demands against the real world
the pleasure principle, seeking immediate satisfaction of every urge
questions.explanation: Freud described the ego as working on the reality principle, finding realistic ways to meet the id's urges while respecting the superego's moral standards. The pleasure principle drives the id, and internalised moral values make up the superego.

questions.stem: Why do many psychologists argue that Freud's theory of personality is hard to test scientifically?
options: Its key processes are unconscious and can explain any outcome after the event
It was developed using large laboratory experiments that no one has been able to repeat
It describes only observable behaviour, so it ignores thoughts and feelings
It depends on brain imaging technology that was not available to Freud
questions.explanation: Because the id, ego and superego and the defence mechanisms are unconscious, almost any behaviour can be explained after it happens, so the theory is difficult to falsify. Freud built his ideas from case studies of patients, not from large experiments.

questions.stem: According to Erik Erikson, the central task of adolescence is to resolve the crisis of:
options: identity versus role confusion
industry versus inferiority
intimacy versus isolation
autonomy versus shame and doubt
questions.explanation: Erikson's fifth stage, in adolescence, is identity versus role confusion, in which young people explore roles and values to form a stable ego identity. Industry versus inferiority is the school-age stage before it, and intimacy versus isolation follows in early adulthood.

questions.stem: Erikson's idea of ego identity differs from Freud's view of personality mainly because Erikson:
options: emphasised social relationships and development across the whole life span
argued that identity is set by inherited traits and cannot be changed by experience
believed that sexual urges in early childhood fix adult identity
claimed that identity is a set of conditioned responses to rewards
questions.explanation: Erikson kept some psychodynamic ideas but stressed social and cultural influences and saw development continuing through eight stages to old age. Freud's psychosexual stages focus on early childhood and sexual energy.

questions.stem: Albert Bandura defined self-efficacy as:
options: a person's overall judgement of their own worth and value as a person
the gap between who a person is and who they would like to be
a person's membership of groups that give them a social identity
a person's belief in their ability to succeed at a particular task
questions.explanation: Self-efficacy is task-specific: belief that one can carry out the actions needed to succeed. Overall judgement of worth is self-esteem, which is a different concept; a student can have high self-esteem but low self-efficacy for calculus.

questions.stem: Which experience would Bandura predict is the strongest source of self-efficacy for learning to swim?
options: Being told by a friend that swimming is easy
Feeling calm before getting into the pool
Successfully swimming a short distance unaided
Watching an Olympic swimmer on television
questions.explanation: Bandura named mastery experiences, actually succeeding, as the most powerful source of self-efficacy. Vicarious experience works best when the model is similar to the learner, and verbal persuasion and physiological states are weaker sources.

questions.stem: In Tajfel and Turner's social identity theory, social identity is:
options: the set of personal traits that make a person different from everyone else they know
the impression that other people form of a person on first meeting them
the roles that a person plays in their family as they grow older
the part of a person's self-concept that comes from their group memberships
questions.explanation: Social identity theory proposes that people define themselves partly through the groups they belong to, such as a school, team or nationality. Personal identity, built from individual traits, is the other part of the self-concept.

questions.stem: Which list gives the three processes in social identity theory in the order they occur?
options: Social categorisation, social comparison, social identification
Social categorisation, social identification, social comparison
Social comparison, social categorisation, social identification
Social identification, social comparison, social categorisation
questions.explanation: People first sort themselves and others into groups (categorisation), then take on the identity of their group (identification), then compare their group with others (comparison). Comparison favouring the in-group helps to maintain self-esteem.

questions.stem: After her netball team wins the grand final, Gemma wears her team scarf everywhere and talks about how much better her club is than its rivals. Social identity theory explains this as:
options: satisfying a physiological need before moving up to esteem needs
boosting self-esteem through a favourable comparison of her in-group
reducing cognitive load by relying on a stereotype of the other club
resolving the crisis of identity versus role confusion for good
questions.explanation: Social identity theory holds that people gain self-esteem from their groups, so a successful in-group is displayed proudly and compared favourably with out-groups. Erikson's identity crisis and Maslow's needs are different theories.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes gender identity from gender expression?
options: Identity is the set of social expectations for each gender; expression is purely biological
Identity and expression are both terms for the behaviour a society expects of a sex
Identity is a person's inner sense of their gender; expression is how they present it
Identity is how a person dresses and acts; expression is their inner sense of gender
questions.explanation: Gender identity is a person's internal sense of their own gender, while gender expression is how they show gender outwardly through clothing, appearance and behaviour. The behaviours a society expects of people of a given gender are called gender roles.

questions.stem: In one community it is expected that women do most of the cooking and men do most of the outdoor work. These expectations are examples of:
options: gender identity
self-efficacy
ego identity
gender roles
questions.explanation: Gender roles are the socially shared expectations about how people of each gender should behave, and they vary across cultures and over time. Gender identity is an individual's inner sense of their own gender.

questions.stem: Theory of mind is the ability to:
options: recognise one's own reflection in a mirror and touch a mark placed on one's own face
hold about seven items in short-term memory while working on a problem
judge one's own worth by comparing oneself with members of other groups
understand that other people have beliefs and knowledge different from one's own
questions.explanation: Theory of mind is understanding that others have their own mental states, including false beliefs. Recognising oneself in a mirror is self-recognition, tested by the mirror (mark) test, which is a different ability that appears earlier.

questions.stem: In the Sally-Anne test, Sally puts a marble in a basket and leaves; Anne moves it to a box. A child who passes says Sally will look in the basket. What does passing show?
options: The child can conserve the number of marbles present
The child recognises Sally as a member of their group
The child understands that Sally holds a false belief
The child can remember where the marble is now hidden
questions.explanation: To pass, the child must set aside what they know (the marble is in the box) and predict from what Sally believes, which is a false belief. Simply remembering the marble's real location would lead to the wrong answer.

questions.stem: Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith (1985) gave the Sally-Anne test to autistic children, typically developing children and children with Down syndrome. Why was the Down syndrome group included?
options: To make sure the experimenters did not know which of the groups each child belonged to
To give every child in the study an equal chance of being in each condition
To measure how much the children's answers changed when the test was repeated
To check whether failure was due to general intellectual delay rather than autism
questions.explanation: Most children with Down syndrome passed while most autistic children, who had higher average verbal ability, failed, suggesting the difficulty was specific to theory of mind rather than general delay. The group acted as a comparison for intellectual disability.

questions.stem: In the mirror (mark) test, a researcher secretly puts a spot of rouge on a toddler's nose and places the toddler in front of a mirror. Which response indicates self-recognition?
options: The toddler looks behind the mirror for another child
The toddler touches the mark on their own nose
The toddler reaches out to touch the mirror image
The toddler smiles at the reflection in the mirror
questions.explanation: Touching the mark on one's own face shows the child understands the reflection is themselves. Reaching for or looking behind the mirror suggests the child treats the image as another child. Most children pass between about 18 and 24 months.

questions.stem: A researcher concludes that an animal that fails the mirror test has no sense of self. Which is the most valid criticism of this conclusion?
options: The test relies on vision and interest in one's face, so failing may not mean no self-awareness
The test cannot be used with animals because it was designed only for human infants at first
The test measures theory of mind rather than self-recognition, so it answers the wrong question
The test produces different results every time, so it cannot be used for any conclusion at all
questions.explanation: The mark test depends on an animal using sight and caring about a mark on its body; species that rely on smell, or ignore marks, may fail despite some self-awareness. Gallup first developed the test with chimpanzees, so it was not designed only for infants.

questions.stem: Bracken's Multidimensional Self-Concept Scale measures self-concept in six domains rather than as a single score. Which list names those domains?
options: Physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, academic, family
Continuity, distinctiveness, efficacy, esteem, family, physical
Social, competence, affect, academic, family, physical
Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism, physical
questions.explanation: Bracken's scale assesses social, competence, affect, academic, family and physical self-concept, reflecting the view that people can feel quite differently about themselves in different areas of life. The second list is mostly the Big Five personality traits.

questions.stem: Mia scores high on academic self-concept but low on physical self-concept. What does this suggest about measuring self-concept?
options: Her results show she is high in neuroticism and low in openness
A single overall score could hide large differences between domains
Her scores are unreliable because self-concept must be the same in all areas
She has low self-efficacy for every task, so her academic score is invalid
questions.explanation: A multidimensional model expects people to evaluate themselves differently across areas, so averaging into one score would lose useful information. Different domain scores do not make the measure unreliable.

questions.stem: According to labelling theory, a student who is repeatedly called a troublemaker may come to:
options: see themselves that way and behave in line with the label
reject the label and become more distinctive from the group
lose all memory of being called a troublemaker in the past
improve their behaviour so that the label no longer applies
questions.explanation: Labelling theory proposes that labels applied by others can be absorbed into a person's self-concept and shape later behaviour, a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy. Some people do resist labels, but the theory's prediction is that the label tends to stick.

questions.stem: Glynis Breakwell's identity process theory proposes that identity is guided by principles. When a principle such as continuity is blocked, for example by losing a long-held job, the person experiences:
options: role confusion, which can only be resolved in a later life stage
cognitive dissonance, which is reduced by changing one of the conflicting beliefs
incongruence, which disappears when given unconditional regard
identity threat, and uses coping strategies to restore the principle
questions.explanation: Breakwell's theory names continuity, distinctiveness, self-efficacy and self-esteem as guiding principles; when change prevents one being met, identity threat results and the person copes to restore it. Role confusion and incongruence belong to Erikson and Rogers.

questions.stem: Which list names the Big Five personality traits described by Costa and McCrae?
options: Sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic, neurotic
Self-esteem, self-efficacy, self-image, ideal self, identity
Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism
Introversion, sensing, thinking, judging, perceiving
questions.explanation: The Big Five (often remembered as OCEAN) are openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Sensing, thinking, judging and perceiving are Myers-Briggs categories, which are not a scientific trait model.

questions.stem: A person who is organised, dependable and plans ahead would score high on which Big Five trait?
options: Conscientiousness
Agreeableness
Openness
Extraversion
questions.explanation: Conscientiousness describes being organised, careful, reliable and goal-directed. Agreeableness is about being cooperative and trusting, openness about curiosity and imagination, and extraversion about sociability and energy from others.

questions.stem: Why do psychologists regard the Big Five as a more scientific model of personality than the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator?
options: It measures traits on continuous scales with good test-retest reliability
It sorts every person into one of sixteen types that never change
It was developed from case studies of a small number of patients
It gives each person a single score for their overall personality
questions.explanation: Big Five scores sit on continuous scales, are fairly stable on retesting and predict outcomes such as job performance, and the model was derived from large data sets. Sorting people into fixed types is the Myers-Briggs approach that critics question.

questions.stem: Many people who take the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator twice, a few weeks apart, receive a different type. This is evidence of poor:
options: informed consent
test-retest reliability
inter-rater reliability
random allocation
questions.explanation: A reliable test gives consistent results when the same person is tested again under similar conditions. If many people change type within weeks, the test has low test-retest reliability. Inter-rater reliability concerns agreement between different scorers.

questions.stem: The Myers-Briggs measures preferences on continuous scales but then places each person on one side of a cut-off, such as introvert or extravert. Why is this a problem for validity?
options: Most people score near the middle, so two similar people can be given opposite types
Continuous scales cannot be scored, so the cut-off has no effect on anyone's type
The cut-off is chosen at random each time the test is scored, so it has no reliability at all
Splitting scores into two types always increases the accuracy of the measurement
questions.explanation: Scores on traits such as introversion and extraversion cluster around the middle, so a person just either side of the cut-off is labelled as opposite types despite being almost identical. Forcing continuous traits into categories loses information.

questions.stem: Students are given the same vague personality description, such as 'You have a great need for others to like you', and most rate it as highly accurate for them. This is called the:
options: Pygmalion effect
Barnum (Forer) effect
enclothed cognition effect
fundamental attribution error
questions.explanation: The Barnum or Forer effect is the tendency to accept vague, general statements as specifically true of oneself. It helps explain why horoscopes, online 'which character are you' quizzes and some personality tests feel accurate even when they are not valid.

questions.stem: An online quiz, 'Which movie character are you?', is shared by millions of people. Which is the strongest reason it cannot be treated as a valid measure of personality?
options: It gives results instantly, so it cannot have been checked for informed consent
There is no evidence that its results relate to how people actually think and behave
Too many people have taken it, so the sample is too large to give useful results
It is completed online, and online questionnaires can never measure personality
questions.explanation: Validity means a test measures what it claims to; a quiz with no evidence linking its results to real behaviour or established trait measures has not been validated. Online delivery and large numbers of users are not in themselves the problem.

questions.stem: A company decides to hire only applicants whose personality test shows a particular 'leader' type. Which is the most important ethical and scientific concern?
options: Personality has no influence at all on how people behave at work, whatever is measured
The company cannot score the test itself, so the results must be inaccurate for everyone
Decisions about people are being made on a test that may lack evidence of validity for the job
Applicants have to answer questions, which always breaches their right to confidentiality
questions.explanation: Using a test to make high-stakes decisions is only fair if the test is reliable and validly predicts job performance; type-based tests have weak evidence for this and may disadvantage some groups. Personality does relate to work behaviour, so saying it has no influence is wrong.

questions.stem: Many programs in the 1980s and 1990s aimed to raise students' self-esteem to improve their marks. A major 2003 review by Baumeister and colleagues concluded that:
options: raising self-esteem reliably caused large gains in academic results
self-esteem and school results were completely unrelated in every study
low self-esteem was the main cause of poor marks in most students
high self-esteem does not appear to cause better school performance
questions.explanation: The review found only modest correlations, and evidence suggested good performance may raise self-esteem rather than the reverse; boosting self-esteem did not reliably improve marks. This shows how a popular idea can spread through schools ahead of the evidence.

questions.stem: A psychologist explains identity in terms of a person's free will, subjective experience and striving to reach their potential. This reflects the:
options: biological perspective
psychoanalytic perspective
socio-cultural perspective
humanistic perspective
questions.explanation: The humanistic perspective, associated with Rogers and Maslow, emphasises free will, personal growth and each person's subjective experience. The psychoanalytic perspective stresses unconscious forces, and the socio-cultural perspective stresses group and cultural influences.

questions.stem: Adam and Galinsky (2012) found that participants wearing a lab coat described as a doctor's coat paid closer attention than those wearing the same coat described as a painter's coat. This effect is called:
options: the Barnum effect
social facilitation
the mirror effect
enclothed cognition
questions.explanation: Enclothed cognition is the idea that clothes affect thinking through both their symbolic meaning and the experience of wearing them. Because the coats were identical, the difference came from the meaning attached to them. Later replications have been mixed.

questions.stem: In the doctor's-coat versus painter's-coat condition of the enclothed cognition study, what was the independent variable?
options: The description given to the coat
The number of differences spotted
The colour and fit of the coat
The age of the participants
questions.explanation: The coats were physically the same; only the label (doctor's or painter's) was changed by the researchers, so that is the independent variable. The number of differences spotted between pictures was the dependent variable, measuring sustained attention.

questions.stem: A Year 11 class wants to investigate whether personality relates to how many friends people have. Which plan is the most ethical and valid for school students?
options: Diagnose classmates' personality types by watching them secretly, without telling them
Ask friends to rate each other's personalities aloud in class so results are recorded quickly
Use an established Big Five questionnaire anonymously, with informed consent and the right to withdraw
Use an online 'which character are you' quiz and publish each classmate's result with their name
questions.explanation: A validated questionnaire improves validity, and anonymity, informed consent and the right to withdraw protect participants. Publishing named results, secret observation and public rating risk harm and breach confidentiality.
